title: Product Size Reference Photo to Show Scale | AIVideosUGC
description: Put your product next to a familiar object so shoppers can judge its size at a glance. AI scale photos for listings and ads, from one photo.
h1: Product Size Reference Photo Beside One Familiar Object
lead: A tote's size is easier to trust when a familiar object sits beside it. Open a size layout, use one photo of the whole tote, and place a closed notebook next to it.

steps.d: Use a photo that shows the whole tote, edge to edge. The listing photo is enough, and you skip a second shoot.
Pick an object shoppers understand, such as a closed notebook beside the tote. An avatar can say how it packs, in words you edit.
Save a square for the listing, or a 9:16 clip that says the size aloud. Shoppers can judge the tote before they read the details.

faq.q: What is a size video ad template?
faq.a: It shows the whole item next to one object shoppers already understand. A daypack beside a carry-on outline makes the pack size obvious, and you skip building that comparison yourself on a studio table.

faq.q: How does a size template become a finished file?
faq.a: You leave with a file that shows the scale. Put the full thermos in the layout, choose a phone as the reference, and download the square. An avatar can say the size from a script you edit.

faq.q: Why a template instead of filming a scale setup?
faq.a: Building a scale setup means finding the prop and the time. When you want the thermos beside a bowl instead of a canister, you name the new object in this layout and render again.
Sellers whose product is hard to judge from a photo alone. A jewelry shop showing a ring, and the freelancer who makes ads for that shop, both need the comparison to be obvious.

faq.q: Can I show scale if I have never edited?
faq.a: Yes. One full photo and the three steps are enough to show scale. You name the familiar object, and the layout places it.

faq.q: Which products are hard to size from a photo alone?
faq.a: Small goods and soft goods. A compact, a scarf, and a folded towel can each sit beside one familiar object so the scale reads without a ruler.

faq.q: Can I start from photos and clips I shot?
faq.a: Yes. Your logo can mark the corner, and the ring should be the one from your bench photo. A clip of the band is optional, and you can add up to 7 reference images.

faq.q: Which platforms can the file go to?
faq.a: The square still belongs on the product page. A tall 9:16 cut can run on TikTok, and 1:1 can sit in the shop grid. Wide 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4 can cover a YouTube or LinkedIn placement.

faq.q: Do size templates sit on a paid subscription?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month with 200 credits, Pro is $35 with 300, and Premium is $63 with 600. Each product photo is 24 credits. A video is 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. The cost shows before the job, and a failed job returns the credits.

faq.q: Can I use the size file in ads and for clients?
faq.a: Yes. Put the square on the product page, run the clip as an ad, or send the file to a client who sells the same scarf.

faq.q: Why use a size template instead of building a comparison yourself?
faq.a: Your effort goes into picking the object shoppers trust. The blanket stays in a layout that already has a place for that object, and you only name what sits beside it.

reviews.h2: Shops Showing Size With One Object
reviews.lead: Each card uses one reference object. None of them replace measured dimensions. These are examples, not customer quotes.

items.d: A bag shop places a daypack beside a carry-on outline as a size hint, and writes the liters in the listing. The picture does not prove it fits the bin.
A bottle shop places a bottle next to an open palm. The hand is a generated size hint, not a photo of a customer.
A notebook shop places a planner beside a closed notebook so the page size is easier to picture.
A jewelry shop places a pendant beside a common coin so the face size is easier to see.
A case shop places a small case next to a phone outline and leaves the millimeters in the text.
A shoe shop places a shoe beside a familiar insole length. Fit still depends on the size chart, not the picture.
A kitchen shop places a canister beside a common jar so capacity is easier to picture.
A pet shop places a bowl beside a familiar mug and writes the real capacity next to the image.
A tool shop places a small driver in a palm so shoppers can see that it is small enough for a pocket.
A lamp shop places a lamp beside a side table for a quick height hint, and keeps the measured height in the listing.
